summary: Eurasian watermilfoil is an underwater plant rooted in lake bottoms that grows quickly into dense beds and surface mats, usually in water 3 to 13 feet deep. The mats shade out native water plants early in the season, leading to fewer invertebrates and native fish, smaller fish spawning areas and slower fish growth, and native waterfowl avoid feeding in it. It also makes boating and swimming difficult, and control costs New York more than half a million dollars a year.
history: Eurasian watermilfoil is native to Eurasia. It is now a major water invader across much of North America; because it looks so much like native watermilfoils, reports from before 1940 may have been mistaken identifications.

handling.text: Cutting and harvesting only gives short-term relief and releases plant fragments that can spread it to new areas, and herbicides can harm other plants and fish. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
